meta_description: One crying-wolf quarter kills the program; alarm governance is a first-class design goal.

blocks.x: One crying-wolf quarter kills the program; alarm governance is a first-class design goal.

Predictive maintenance fails socially before it fails statistically is not a slogan; it is a delivery position. Across engagements the pattern repeats: programs that respect this move faster and survive audit; those that do not pay for it later — usually in the audit itself.

items: Failure-mode-driven models beat generic anomaly detection — physics before ML.
Predictions must become work orders with parts reserved, or they are dashboard decorations.
Planner trust (share of predictions actioned) is the KPI that predicts program survival.

blocks.x: Three questions to ask your current vendors

items: What is the classical baseline every proposed capability must beat, measured on identical data?
Who signs the go/no-go gate, and what evidence do they require before signing?
What did you stop last quarter, and what did the stop save us?

blocks.x: The expensive mistake is measurement retrofits: without the baseline locked in week one, every outcome claim becomes an argument instead of an audit, and the program loses its budget defense.

items: falsifiable criteria and locked baselines before build; the demo is the least important artifact.
named owners, run models and escalation paths agreed with the operating team, not for it.
replay trails, control tests and documentation as artifacts of the build — never reconstructed.

blocks.x: Mature programs run above 70% prediction-action rates with downtime down 30-50%.
